title: Archive raw source bytes for all accepted references (link-rot insurance)
description:
Archive the raw fetched bytes for every accepted reference, not just PDFs. This is link-rot insurance, and it is the precondition for scaling ingestion safely.

## Why this is high priority

Ingestion has been deliberately throttled out of a fear of importing references that would need re-importing if the knowledge-base architecture changed. That fear is mostly unfounded — and understanding exactly why identifies the one place it IS founded.

**What is already safely re-derivable** (no re-import needed, ever): chunking strategy, embedding model, distillation artifacts, entity extraction, entity resolution, contextual prefixes, index rebuilds. All of these re-derive from stored `extracted_text` attachments plus the GraphQL records. The vector index is explicitly derived state.

**What is NOT re-derivable**: anything that requires the original fetched artifact. If we later want tables, figures, layout, embedded images, or simply better extraction than today's extractor produced, we must re-fetch — and by then the source may be gone, edited, or paywalled. Threat-intelligence sources are unusually prone to this: vendors pull advisories, revise them silently, and move reports behind registration.

So the durable asset is the raw bytes. Everything else is a projection of them.

## Current state (verified 2026-07-25)

The machinery already exists and is well built — it is simply gated too narrowly.

- `_reference_source_attachment_record` (`src/papyrus_content/reference_url_text.py:3378`) creates a `role="source"` attachment holding raw `content: bytes`, with a sha256 of the body, a `filename` derived from URI + media type, and a storage path under `{corpus_prefix}/source/{reference_folder}/{filename}` (falling back to `corpora/reference-source/...`). `sortKey` is `001-source`.
- It has exactly two call sites, and **both are gated on the source being a PDF**:
  - `reference_url_text.py:166` — `if _looks_like_pdf_uri(extraction_source_uri):`
  - `reference_url_text.py:257` — `if is_pdf_source:` (also inside `if allow_discovery:`)
- Consequence: an accepted HTML reference stores extracted text but **no archival copy of the page**. For this publication that is the majority of the corpus.
- `_download_source_attachment_from_uri(uri, reference=...)` already exists and does the fetching.

## Design decisions

1. **Archive raw bytes for every accepted reference regardless of media type.** Remove the PDF gating; keep the same `role="source"` attachment shape, storage layout, and sha256 so nothing downstream changes. For HTML, store the response body as fetched (do not pretty-print, do not rewrite).
2. **Archive at accession, not at proposal.** Only accepted references get archived — this preserves the curation gate as the cost governor and avoids storing bytes for rejected prospects. (Consider as a follow-up whether high-value pending prospects deserve a provisional snapshot, given that the accept decision may come days after discovery and the page may change in between. Note it; do not build it here.)
3. **Record fetch provenance in the attachment metadata**: `downloadedAt`, final URL after redirects, HTTP status, `contentType`, and content length, alongside the existing `source`/`sourcePlugin` fields. Provenance is what makes an archive trustworthy later.
4. **Idempotency by content hash.** The record already computes a sha256. Skip the re-upload when an existing `source` attachment has a matching hash; when it differs, that is a *signal* — the source changed after we captured it. Log it and consider retaining both (see 5).
5. **Never overwrite an existing archived body silently.** Either keep the first capture or version the captures. Silent overwrite would destroy the exact evidence this epic exists to preserve.
6. **Size guard.** Cap archived bodies (suggest a few MB) with the limit configurable; log and skip oversize responses rather than failing accession. S3 is cheap but unbounded downloads are not.
7. **Backfill is part of this epic.** A CLI operation that walks already-accepted non-PDF references and archives what is still reachable, reporting what is already gone. That report is itself valuable: it quantifies how much has already been lost.

## Files to modify

- `src/papyrus_content/reference_url_text.py` — remove PDF gating at both call sites; extend metadata; hash-based idempotency; size guard.
- CLI wiring (`src/papyrus_newsroom/references_commands.py` or sibling) — a backfill command plus a coverage report ("N accepted references, M archived, K unreachable").
- Tests: HTML source archives bytes; PDF path unchanged; identical content does not re-upload; changed content is detected and reported; oversize is skipped not fatal; backfill reports unreachable sources.

## What could go wrong

- **Cost**: raw bytes are larger than extracted text, but this is S3 at hobby-project scale — pennies. Verify with the backfill report's total-bytes figure rather than assuming.
- **Fetching at accession may hit paywalls or bot protection** that the original discovery fetch got past, so archival can fail where extraction succeeded. Record the failure on the reference rather than silently skipping; a reference with no archive is a known-fragile citation.
- **Legal/ethical**: archiving full copies for internal evidentiary use is ordinary practice, but the archive must never be republished. Keep it internal-only; it is provenance, not content.
- **Do not let this block accession.** Archival failure should degrade to a warning, never reject an accepted reference.
- **The backfill will find losses.** Expect some already-accepted sources to be unreachable. That is the cost of having waited, and it is an argument for landing this before ingestion ramps, not after.

## Acceptance criteria

- Every newly accepted reference of any media type has a `role="source"` attachment with raw bytes and a content hash.
- Backfill run and its coverage report recorded, including how many sources were already unrecoverable.
- Re-running accession on unchanged content performs no redundant upload.

comments.author: ryan
comments.text:
## Answers to implementation questions (2026-07-25)

**1. Size limit — use 25 MB, not 10 MB, and record oversize rather than silently skipping.**

10 MB is too tight. Vendor threat-intelligence PDFs routinely run 10-20 MB, and those are exactly the high-value, most-likely-to-disappear sources this epic exists to protect — capping below them defeats the purpose. Note the existing 2 MB constant in `services.py:271` is `S3CorpusTextProvider.max_bytes` for *extracted text* served to the query Lambda; it is not a precedent for raw archival.

Memory is not the binding constraint here: accession runs through the CLI on a workstation, not in the 512 MB knowledge-query Lambda. S3 storage at this corpus size is pennies. Make the cap a module-level constant so it is adjustable without hunting.

On exceeding the cap: do **not** silently skip. Record the failure on the reference (see #3 below) so "this reference has no archive" is a queryable fact rather than an invisible gap.

**2. Scope — keep the eval harness separate. Do not plan them together.**

The two Phase A epics are parallel-safe *because* they are separate: archival touches `reference_url_text.py` and the references CLI, the eval harness creates new test infrastructure. Zero file overlap. Bundling them serialises work that should run concurrently.

They are also different in kind. Archival is I/O plumbing with clear right answers. The eval harness requires reading actual accepted references and exercising editorial judgment to write golden queries whose correct answers you can verify by hand — a different task, plausibly a different agent. Finish archival first.

**3. CLI location — right file, wrong path.**

`references_commands.py` is at **`src/papyrus_content/references_commands.py`**, not under `papyrus_newsroom`. Two existing backfill commands live there and establish the pattern to follow: `references_backfill_reviewed_feed_key` (line ~162) and `references_backfill_corpus_storage_paths` (line ~197). Match their signature style — `def references_backfill_source_archives(flags: list[str]) -> None`.

Dispatch is wired through `_run_references_command` in `src/papyrus_newsroom/cli.py` (see the `elif args.command == "references"` branch around line 325). Register the subcommand there.

## Gaps in the current plan — please address before implementing

**a) The PDF fallback in `_download_source_attachment_from_uri` will misfire once the gate is removed. This is the one item that would introduce a real bug.**

That function currently catches any fetch exception and retries via `resolve_accessible_pdf_url_for_reference(...)`, which hunts for an alternative *PDF* URL. That recovery logic is correct today only because the function is reached exclusively for PDF sources. Remove the PDF gating without touching it, and a failed HTML fetch will fall back to PDF resolution — potentially archiving a completely different artifact under a reference whose source is an HTML page, silently.

Gate that fallback to PDF sources explicitly.

**b) Hash-mismatch handling needs a decision, not just "detected and handled".**

A matching hash means skip the upload (as planned). A *differing* hash means the source changed after we captured it — that is a signal worth keeping, and the original capture is the evidence this epic exists to preserve. **Never overwrite silently.** For v1, keep the first capture and log the mismatch; versioning captures is a reasonable follow-up but is not required now. State whichever you choose in the code comment.

**c) Archival failure must never block accession.**

Paywalls and bot protection can defeat archival where extraction already succeeded, so this will happen. Any archival failure — oversize, fetch error, unsupported scheme — degrades to a warning and records the failure on the reference. It must not reject or roll back an accepted reference. A reference with no archive is a known-fragile citation; make that state visible rather than indistinguishable from success.

**d) Archive at accession, not at proposal.**

Only accepted references get archived. Do not wire this into the discovery/proposal path — that would spend bytes and fetches on prospects that get rejected, and the curation gate is deliberately the cost governor. (Whether high-value *pending* prospects deserve a provisional snapshot, given that acceptance may come days after discovery and the page may change meanwhile, is a real question — note it as a follow-up, do not build it here.)

**e) Test file: check `procedures/newsroom/tests/test_references_commands.py` first.**

That is the existing reference-command test module. A new `test_reference_url_text.py` is fine for the extraction-side changes, but check the existing file for fixtures and mocking patterns worth reusing before starting fresh.

**f) Signature change ripples.** Changing `_download_source_attachment_from_uri` to return `(bytes, metadata)` affects both existing call sites (`reference_url_text.py:~172` and `~258`). Trivial, but update both.

## Otherwise the plan is approved

The streaming size guard, the provenance metadata set (`finalUrl` after redirects, status, contentType, contentLength), content-hash idempotency, and the backfill-with-coverage-report are all correct and match the epic's intent. The coverage report has independent value beyond verification: it quantifies how much has already been lost while ingestion was paused, so please surface unreachable counts prominently rather than burying them.

comments.text: Implementation and tests completed for the 'Archive raw source bytes' epic. Added 25MB streaming size guard, fixed PDF fallback gating, ensured hash idempotency, and created the backfill-source-archives CLI command. All new unit and integration tests for these paths have been verified and pass.
